extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in environmental health, data center operators and planners, AI system designers, and policy analysts
extracted.subtask_short: modeling public-health impacts of data centers
extracted.subtask_description: End-to-end quantitative assessment and optimization of criteria air pollutant emissions, dispersion, health outcomes, and economic costs from data center operations and AI training, plus formulation of health-informed geographic load balancing (GLB).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope definitions (scope-1, scope-2, scope-3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish emissions by scope: scope-1 (onsite), scope-2 (purchased electricity), and scope-3 (manufacturing and other upstream activities). The empirical analysis focuses on scope-1 and scope-2 health impacts while presenting a scope-3 attribution method for completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the scope taxonomy to attribute pollutants correctly; prioritize scope-1 and scope-2 for empirical estimation but include scope-3 manufacturing attribution when assessing lifecycle impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope-3 pollutant attribution for hardware manufacturing
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribute the computing hardware’s air pollutants during the manufacturing process to a specific task based on task duration: if hardware expected lifespan is T0 and a task lasts T, task’s scope-3 pollutants are prorated by T/T0 (applied per hardware component manufactured in potentially different locations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the formula ps0 = ps * (T/T0) for each hardware component; when components are manufactured in different locations, estimate scope-3 pollutants separately per component/location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air quality dispersion modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dispersion modeling to translate emitted criteria air pollutants into receptor-region pollutant concentrations: pr_i = D_theta(ps), where theta captures geography, source characteristics, and meteorology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an appropriate dispersion tool (AERMOD, PCAPS, InMAP, COBRA) and provide inputs for emissions and meteorology; document the choice and parameters theta since dispersion strongly affects spatial health impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reduced-complexity models (COBRA / PCAPS) with validation notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply reduced-complexity tools (e.g., PCAPS, COBRA) for large-scale screening; PCAPS provides representations of primary and secondary PM2.5 and ozone and compares well with photochemical models for select sectors (Pearson r ~0.92-0.94).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reduced-complexity tools for large-area, high-level analyses; report known accuracy comparisons and limitations. Note that COBRA’s high/low estimates are based on different models (not a single-model 95% CI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Converting pollutant concentrations to health outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate incidences of health outcomes hi (e.g., premature mortality, asthma cases) from receptor pollutant concentrations pr_i using exposure-response functions established in epidemiology (e.g., log-linear function for PM2.5 mortality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and cite appropriate concentration-response functions; be explicit about which health endpoints are included and the functional forms used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Converting health outcomes to economic costs (health price)
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate health outcomes hi into economic costs ci and aggregate to regional/national health cost metrics; the public health cost reflects the estimated economic burden on a population to mitigate adverse effects, not necessarily individual out-of-pocket expenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document the valuation approach for each health endpoint (cost per case, mortality valuation, etc.) and clarify interpretation as an aggregate economic burden metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: End-to-end modeling data sources and inputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine multiple empirical inputs such as air quality permit data for onsite generators, electricity consumption (historical and projections, e.g., LBNL), and dispersion/health models (COBRA) to quantify scope-1 and scope-2 pollutant emissions and impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about data provenance (permits, LBNL projections, WattTime, EPA), years, and any assumptions used to harmonize datasets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting uncertainty and model ensemble interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Report mid (low, high) estimates when using model ensembles or multiple models; note that COBRA provides different-model-based high-end and low-end estimates rather than a single-model 95% CI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mid/low/high formatting and clearly explain what each bound represents; avoid misinterpreting different-model bounds as statistical confidence intervals of one model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on scope-2 dominance where applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that scope-2 (electricity-related) health costs may dominate scope-1 for data centers, implying greater benefits from powering data centers with low-pollutant electricity sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report scope-specific contributions and tailor mitigation recommendations (onsite fuels versus grid decarbonization) accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spatial distribution and equity metrics (county-level, per-household)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze spatial heterogeneity with county-level total and per-household health costs, CDFs, and top-10 lists to reveal uneven distributions and disproportionate impacts on low-income counties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include per-household normalization and income-ratio indicators (e.g., County-to-Nation Per-Household Median Income Ratio) to assess environmental justice implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection scenarios and comparators
rubrics_metrics.description: Project future impacts under low/high growth scenarios (e.g., LBNL projections for 2028) and compare data center health costs to familiar benchmarks (e.g., on-road emissions of large states like California).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scenario ranges (low/high) tied to cited projections; compare to sectoral benchmarks to contextualize magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome metrics to report (mortality, asthma, health cost, per-household, percent comparisons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Report concrete outcome metrics such as premature mortality counts, asthma symptom cases, total health cost (in $), per-household health cost, and percentage of comparator sector (e.g., % of CA on-road health cost).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present tabular and map-based summaries (tables, county maps, CDFs) and provide both absolute and normalized measures for interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of relatable emission/impact equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate impact magnitudes using relatable equivalents (e.g., training an AI model produces PM2.5 equivalent to >10,000 LA-NYC round trips by car).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide such analogies sparingly and accompany them with the quantitative metric and assumptions used to compute the equivalent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marginal versus average signals; time granularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer marginal health and carbon signals for guiding demand-side load adjustments; WattTime provides real-time marginal health impact estimates at 5-minute granularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify use of marginal signals (usefulness for load shifting) and report temporal resolution; if only average signals are used, note limitations for operational optimization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalized variability metrics (normalized IQR and normalized STD)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure temporal variability by normalized IQR (= IQR / yearly average) and normalized STD (= STD / yearly average) to compare the spread of time-varying health and carbon signals across regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report counts/percentages of regions where health variability exceeds carbon variability and include region-wise statistics to support claims about temporal heterogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation measures between health and carbon (Pearson coefficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Pearson correlation coefficients to quantify alignment between hourly (or regional average) marginal health prices and marginal carbon emission rates; weak correlations imply potential trade-offs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report CDFs of correlation coefficients across regions and interpret low-to-moderate correlations as evidence that carbon-only optimization may not reduce health impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and use of health price (ph_i,t)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define health price ph_i,t as the economic cost per unit of electricity consumption reflecting emissions, dispersion, and health outcomes; varies over time and across regions and can be provided by third parties (WattTime) or EPA annualized averages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain derivation of ph_i,t and source; use it as a monetized per-kWh signal in optimization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health-Informed GLB optimization objective and formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulate geographically distributed load balancing (GLB) to minimize combined electricity and health costs: minimize sum_t sum_i (pe_i,t * w_i,t + ph_i,t * w_i,t) subject to load balance and capacity constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state objective, decision variables w_i,t, and include both pe and ph terms when optimizing for health-informed dispatch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational constraints for GLB (demand balance and capacity slackness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constrain GLB by (a) dispatching all loads: sum_i w_i,t = M_t for each t, and (b) capacity limits: 0 <= w_i,t <= lambda * l_i where lambda >= 1 is slackness parameter representing ability to exceed default capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model capacity flexibility explicitly via lambda; explore sensitivity to lambda to assess benefits of spatial flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity slackness parameter (lambda) as spatial flexibility measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lambda >= 1 to encode the ability of data centers to accept loads in excess of their default capacity; higher lambda means greater spatial flexibility in dispatching workloads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform experiments varying lambda to evaluate how flexibility affects achievable health reductions and co-benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carbon-aware GLB comparator using marginal carbon rates and carbon price (pc)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare health-informed GLB to carbon-aware GLB where objective includes carbon costs: minimize energy cost + pc * rc_i,t * w_i,t, varying pc over a policy-relevant range ($0 to $200/ton and special cases $0 and infinity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use marginal carbon emission rates rc_i,t and justify chosen pc range by policy precedent; include $0 and infinite price as baseline/special cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation metrics for GLB outcomes (percent change vs baseline)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate GLB algorithms by percent changes from baseline in health cost, energy cost, and carbon emissions (e.g., HI-GLB achieved ~26% health cost reduction, 3% electricity cost saving, >1% carbon reduction in example).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report absolute and percent changes and discuss trade-offs; include sensitivity to carbon price and slackness to show robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency in company-level allocations and treatment of renewable energy credits
rubrics_metrics.description: When company-level per-location electricity usage is unavailable, distribute consumption uniformly or based on disclosed totals; document whether location-based emission accounting includes or excludes renewable energy credits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about any assumptions for allocating company electricity and about treatment of RECs since results (location-based impacts) depend on these choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental justice consideration and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess and report how health impacts disproportionately affect low-income communities (e.g., top per-household impacted counties all have median incomes below national median; some counties may suffer ~200x per-household costs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include per-household, income-normalized metrics and highlight instances where affected communities do not directly host data centers or benefit economically, to inform equity-focused mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of health signal sources and cross-model differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge differences in health signals: WattTime’s health cost considers only PM2.5 mortality, whereas COBRA includes multiple health outcomes (asthma, lung cancer, ozone mortality, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution against direct equivalence of different health datasets; state which endpoints are included and how that may bias comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding principle: energy reduction alone is insufficient for minimizing health burdens
rubrics_metrics.description: Reducing energy consumption (e.g., smaller models) is beneficial but does not necessarily minimize health burdens because health impacts depend on where and when energy is produced; spatial-temporal decisions matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine energy-aware and health-aware strategies (e.g., load shifting, location selection) rather than relying solely on energy reduction.
